A lot of the discussion around the shooting has focused on the "2nd Amendment Right" and the ensuing gun control "debate."

The writers of the Constitution understood many things, and were very versed in what governance meant for a country.

The "Bill of Rights" is the enumeration of "Human Rights" and sets forth LIMITS on the power of the government to infringe on those Natural Rights.

In summary: the 2nd Amendment doesn't GIVE people the right to bear arms, it ACKNOWLEDGES this inherent fundamental right, and LIMITS the government from taking away that right.

Why does this matter?

Most people in the gun control debate call it the "2nd Amendment Right," and treat it like the government ALLOWS the people this right. As George Carlin says, if the government allows it, it isn't a Right, it is a privilege. And privileges can be taken away.

Calling the Right of Self-Defense an inherent Human Right, means the Constitution doesn't GIVE this right, it actually LIMITS the government in taking that right away.

All of the first 10 Amendments should actually be read as such:

1) it is a Human Right to free speech, and the government is restricted from limiting it

2) it is a Human Right to self-defense, and the government is restricted from limiting it

3) it is a Human Right to decide who gets into your house

4) it is a Human Right to privacy, and the government is limited in how privacy can be violated [this is a lot more important now with FISA and all the NSA bills that have passed]

5) it is a Human Right to due process, and the government is limited

6) it is a Human Right to a speedy trial

7) it is a Human Right to a trial by jury

8) it is a Human Right to not endure cruel and unusual punishment

9) there are many more Human Rights, and just because these are not listed here doesn't mean they exist - just that the ones mentioned above [although they shouldn't] need extra mention

10) if this document doesn't give a power to the federal government, then that power belongs to the people in each of several states.

This matters.
Why "2nd Amendment Right" vs "Right of Self-Defense" matters

Another point that should be made:

At the time of writing the Constitution, the "Bill of Rights" was debated as to whether to even have it.

Such was the thinking: these Human Rights are so common and well-understood that they don't even bear mentioning, [see 9th and 10th Amendment 'catch-alls']

The USA is so fortunate that some of the founders understood government depravity so well, that they actually forced these Amendments to be added.

Imagine a world right now where 200 years ago all of these Rights were well understood and were left out of the explicit list of Rights. People would be of the mindset that there are no Human Rights and that whatever the government gives is the only thing that exists.

If only more people understood this. A good example is the 3rd Amendment. One that is highly unusual to people today. Why is it even there?

Imagine getting a knock at 10pm and a soldier is outside demanding to come in and stay the night.... That really happened prior to the Revolutionary War. The writers of the Constitution were all too experienced with this notion, and it displeased them very much. So much, that they understood that it was a fundamental Human Right to decide who gets to enter a private residence, and so powerful was this thought that it became the 3rd Amendment.

The writers of the Constitution were well aware of how a government abuses power, and also well aware of what fundamental Human Rights were. And here today we have people determined to sabotage their lives because they think the government decides who gets to say or have what...
